youtube.title: Why Did Decca Reject the Beatles?
youtube.description:
The Beatles Decca audition of 1 January 1962 saw the band drive through snow to London and play fifteen songs in about an hour. Decca Records turned them down and signed Brian Poole and the Tremeloes instead. Why did Decca let the Beatles go, and what happened to the Decca tapes afterward?

This documentary follows the audition, the two conflicting accounts of the meeting that ended it, the labels that said no before Decca did, and how the rejected tape itself led the Beatles to EMI. Then it follows Decca's second chance with the Rolling Stones, and where the label and the Beatles' recordings ended up.

{CHAPTERS}

sources.claim: On 4 April 1964 the Beatles held all five top places on the Billboard Hot 100
sources.source: Billboard Hot 100 chart dated 4 April 1964

sources.claim: The Beatles auditioned for Decca on 1 January 1962 and recorded 15 songs in about an hour
sources.source: Mark Lewisohn, The Beatles: All These Years, Vol. 1: Tune In (2013); Lewisohn, The Complete Beatles Recording Sessions (1988)

sources.claim: Decca signed Brian Poole and the Tremeloes, from Dagenham, who auditioned the same day
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: In 1961 EMI and Decca dominated British record releases
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: Decca's record label began in 1929 when stockbroker Edward Lewis took over the Decca gramophone company
sources.source: Decca Records company history; Edward Lewis obituary, The Times, 1980

sources.claim: Decca recorded Tommy Steele (from 1956) and Billy Fury (from 1959)
sources.source: Official Charts Company artist records for Tommy Steele and Billy Fury

sources.claim: Decca's London label issued American recordings in Britain
sources.source: Decca Records company history; Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: Dick Rowe headed Decca's A&R department; Mike Smith was a producer under him
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: Brian Epstein ran the record departments of NEMS, his family's store, a significant Decca customer
sources.source: Brian Epstein, A Cellarful of Noise (1964); Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: Mike Smith watched the Beatles at the Cavern on 13 December 1961 and offered an audition
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: The band drove to London on New Year's Eve in a van driven by Neil Aspinall, around ten hours in snow
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: The session was at Decca Studios, Broadhurst Gardens, West Hampstead, from about 11 a.m.; the producer arrived late
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: Epstein helped choose the set; three of the fifteen songs were Lennon-McCartney originals: Like Dreamers Do, Hello Little Girl, Love of the Loved
sources.source: Lewisohn, The Complete Beatles Recording Sessions (1988); Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: The set included Money, Till There Was You and The Sheik of Araby
sources.source: Lewisohn, The Complete Beatles Recording Sessions (1988)

sources.claim: Biographers describe the band as nervous at the audition
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013); Philip Norman, Shout! (1981)

sources.claim: Mike Smith said he wanted both bands, was told to take one, and chose the Tremeloes as local and easier to work with
sources.source: Mike Smith's later interviews, quoted in Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: Epstein met Dick Rowe and Decca's sales manager in London weeks later to hear the decision
sources.source: Epstein, A Cellarful of Noise (1964); Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: Epstein wrote he was told groups with guitars were on the way out
sources.source: Brian Epstein, A Cellarful of Noise (1964)

sources.claim: Dick Rowe later denied saying it
sources.source: Rowe's later interviews, cited in Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: On 18 December 1961 EMI's marketing manager wrote to Epstein declining the Beatles
sources.source: EMI letter to Brian Epstein, 18 December 1961, reproduced in Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: Pye and Philips also passed in early 1962
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: Epstein had the Decca tape cut to disc at HMV, Oxford Street; an engineer referred him to EMI-owned publisher Ardmore & Beechwood, who led him to George Martin of Parlophone
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013); George Martin, All You Need Is Ears (1979)

sources.claim: George Martin heard the recordings on 13 February 1962 and was not immediately convinced
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013); Martin, All You Need Is Ears (1979)

sources.claim: EMI booked an Abbey Road session for 6 June 1962
sources.source: Lewisohn, The Complete Beatles Recording Sessions (1988)

sources.claim: Lewisohn argues EMI's publishing side's interest in the Lennon-McCartney songs helped push the contract through
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: Ringo Starr replaced Pete Best in August 1962
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013)

sources.claim: Love Me Do was released on 5 October 1962 and reached No. 17 in the UK
sources.source: Official Charts Company; Lewisohn, Recording Sessions (1988)

sources.claim: Please Please Me reached No. 1 on the NME and Melody Maker charts but No. 2 on Record Retailer, now treated as official
sources.source: Official Charts Company; NME and Melody Maker charts, February-March 1963

sources.claim: Capitol had turned down the band's early singles
sources.source: Bruce Spizer, The Beatles' Story on Capitol Records (2000)

sources.claim: Capitol released I Want to Hold Your Hand on 26 December 1963; it reached No. 1 on 1 February 1964
sources.source: Billboard Hot 100, 1 February 1964; Spizer (2000)

sources.claim: Nielsen estimated 73 million viewers for the Beatles on The Ed Sullivan Show, 9 February 1964
sources.source: Nielsen ratings, February 1964

sources.claim: The Beatles had 20 Billboard Hot 100 No. 1s, 1964-1970 (6, 4, 2, 3, 1, 2, 2 by year)
sources.source: Billboard Hot 100 archive

sources.claim: Do You Love Me by Brian Poole and the Tremeloes reached UK No. 1 in October 1963, their only No. 1 together
sources.source: Official Charts Company

sources.claim: The Beatles had 17 UK No. 1 singles
sources.source: Official Charts Company

sources.claim: In May 1963 Rowe sat on a Liverpool talent contest panel with George Harrison, who recommended the Rolling Stones; Decca signed them within days
sources.source: Lewisohn, Tune In (2013); Bill Wyman, Stone Alone (1990)

sources.claim: The Stones stayed on Decca until 1970
sources.source: Wyman, Stone Alone (1990)

sources.claim: The Applejacks released Like Dreamers Do on Decca in 1964
sources.source: Official Charts Company; Decca single release, 1964

sources.claim: The RIAA has certified 183 million Beatles album units in the US, the most of any act
sources.source: RIAA Top Artists (Albums), accessed 2026

sources.claim: Decca was sold to PolyGram in 1980, the year Sir Edward Lewis died
sources.source: The Times obituary of Sir Edward Lewis, January 1980; PolyGram history

sources.claim: Five Decca audition songs were released on Anthology 1 in 1995
sources.source: The Beatles, Anthology 1 liner notes (Apple Corps, 1995)

sources.claim: Universal completed its purchase of EMI's recorded music business on 28 September 2012, Beatles catalogue included
sources.source: Universal Music Group press release, 28 September 2012; European Commission decision, 21 September 2012

sources.claim: Decca is a Universal Music Group label today
